title: Antigen presentation
covers: The features of adaptive immunity, how B and T cells recognize antigen, what antigens are, and how MHC class I and II molecules present peptides to T cells.

items.p: Adaptive immunity starts when antigen-presenting cells, having phagocytosed the pathogen, show it to lymphocytes.

ul: Specificity: one receptor specificity per lymphocyte; tells apart closely related epitopes
Diversity: billions of structures recognized, thanks to variable antigen-binding sites
Memory: second responses are faster, larger and often different in quality
Specialization: a different kind of response for each class of microbe
Self tolerance: no harmful response to self
Self-limitation: the response fades and the system returns to rest (homeostasis)
Clonal expansion: the few specific cells multiply; all progeny carry the same receptor

items.p: Memory is the basis of vaccination. Failed tolerance gives autoimmunity.
B cells use immunoglobulin. Membrane-bound it is the B-cell receptor; secreted it is antibody. It binds native antigen, soluble or on a cell.
T cells use the T-cell receptor. It is never secreted and only sees small peptides held on MHC molecules.

ul: Antibody: 2 identical heavy and 2 identical light chains; two antigen-binding sites
Variable regions bind antigen; the constant region talks to effector cells and molecules
Light chains are κ or λ (normal ratio 2:1; an abnormal ratio suggests a B-cell tumor)
Five classes by heavy chain: IgM (μ), IgA (α), IgD (δ), IgE (ε), IgG (γ)
Affinity: strength of one site. Avidity: combined strength of all sites.
TCR: α and β chain, one binding site, about 30,000 copies per cell; CD3 is part of the complex

items.p: Receptor diversity comes from V(D)J recombination: VDJ for the heavy chain (chromosome 14), VJ for light chains (κ on chromosome 2, λ on 22).

items.note: The slide writes "22 (Igγ)" for the second light-chain locus. It is the lambda (λ) light chain.

ul: Helper (CD4) and cytotoxic (CD8) T cells
Regulatory T cells
NKT cells: remove tumor and stressed cells, help prevent autoimmunity, do not recognize MHC II
γδ T cells: rare, at mucosal and epithelial surfaces, counted as innate; drive inflammation and wound healing

items.p: An antigen is any substance that can provoke an immune response: usually a protein, peptide or polysaccharide.

ul: Epitope: the part of the antigen bound by antibody
Hapten: small molecule that is immunogenic only when bound to a carrier protein (the complex is an adduct)
Exogenous: from outside. Endogenous: made inside the cell (metabolism, virus, intracellular bacteria).
Autoantigen: a self molecule attacked when tolerance fails
Neoantigen: product of a tumor-specific mutation
Native antigen: not yet processed. B cells can bind it; T cells cannot.

items.p: Classical APCs are dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells. Dendritic cells capture most protein antigens.
APCs collect antigen in tissues, travel to the draining lymph node, and present peptides on MHC II to naive T cells.
Humoral immunity (B cells, antibody) handles extracellular microbes and toxins. Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) handles microbes hidden inside cells.
MHC is called HLA in humans. The genes are on chromosome 6.

table: Nucleated cells and platelets (not mature red cells)
APCs: dendritic cells, macrophages, monocytes, B cells
α and β chains, both cross the membrane

items.p: HLA genes are polygenic, polymorphic and codominant. The class III region holds genes such as TNF.

items.note: The slide names the small class I chain "β-macroglobulin". The standard name is β2-microglobulin.

items.p: Endogenous (class I): cytosolic protein is tagged with ubiquitin, cut by the proteasome, moved into the ER by TAP and loaded on class I. Class I does not leave the ER without a peptide.
Exogenous (class II): protein is taken into vesicles and digested. Class II arrives with CLIP in its groove; HLA-DM helps swap CLIP for the peptide.

ul: Signal 1: the TCR binds its peptide on MHC
Signal 2: costimulatory molecules on the T cell bind their ligands on the APC

cards.a: Specificity, diversity, memory, specialization, self tolerance, self-limitation, clonal expansion

cards.q: Why are all cells of a lymphocyte clone specific for the same antigen?
cards.a: Receptor gene rearrangement is an irreversible DNA change passed to all progeny.
Membrane-bound = B-cell receptor; secreted = antibody. The T-cell receptor is never secreted.
2 identical heavy chains + 2 identical light chains (κ or λ), giving two identical binding sites

cards.q: Which antibody region binds antigen, and which interacts with effector cells?
cards.a: Variable (V) regions bind antigen; the constant (C) region is the effector part.

cards.q: Normal κ:λ ratio in humans, and meaning of an abnormal ratio
cards.a: 2:1; an abnormal ratio may indicate a B-cell tumor.
Affinity: strength of a single binding site. Avidity: total strength of all sites together.
Heavy chain: 14. κ light chain: 2. λ light chain: 22.

cards.q: Heavy chain recombination versus light chain recombination
cards.a: Heavy: V-D-J. Light: V-J (no D segment).
α and β chains (disulfide-linked heterodimer), one binding site, associated with CD3

cards.q: What do T cells recognize, compared with B cells?
cards.a: T cells: processed peptide on MHC. B cells: native antigen, no processing needed.
Small molecule that provokes a response only when bound to a carrier protein (complex = adduct)
The surface feature of an antigen that an antibody binds
Dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells

cards.q: Which cells express MHC class I?
cards.a: Nucleated cells and platelets (not mature erythrocytes)

cards.q: Which cells express MHC class II?
cards.a: Antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages, monocytes, B cells

cards.q: MHC I versus MHC II: which T cell?
cards.a: MHC I: CD8 cytotoxic T cells. MHC II: CD4 helper T cells.

cards.q: HLA loci of class I and class II
cards.a: Class I: HLA-A, B, C. Class II: HLA-DR, DP, DQ. Chromosome 6.
One α chain plus β2-microglobulin (encoded on chromosome 15, outside the MHC)
Polygenic, polymorphic, codominant

cards.q: Endogenous antigen pathway in four steps
cards.a: Ubiquitin and proteasome, TAP into the ER, loading on MHC I, display to CD8 T cells
Uptake into vesicles, lysosomal digestion, CLIP exchanged for peptide (HLA-DM), MHC II displays to CD4 T cells

cards.q: What keeps MHC class I in the ER?
cards.a: Lack of a bound peptide: class I leaves the ER only after binding peptide.
Signal 1: TCR binds peptide–MHC. Signal 2: costimulation between T cell and APC.

cards.q: γδ T cells: where and what
cards.a: Mucosal and epithelial sites; innate-like; promote inflammation and wound healing

questions.stem: When innate immunity fails to clear a pathogen, what stimulates the adaptive immune system according to the lecture?

options.A: Complement fragments, after opsonization of the pathogen
options.B: NK cells, after lysis of infected host cells
options.C: Antigen-presenting cells, after phagocytosis of the pathogen
options.D: Memory B cells, after first contact with the pathogen
options.E: Neutrophils, after migration into the draining lymph node

questions.explanation: The adaptive immune system is stimulated by antigen-presenting cells after phagocytosis of the pathogen. A: Complement is an innate effector; the slide names APCs. B: Not the trigger named. D: Memory cells result from an adaptive response. E: APCs carry antigen to lymphoid organs.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties belongs to adaptive but not innate immunity?

options.A: Rapid onset and pattern recognition
options.B: Germline-encoded receptors and non-clonal distribution
options.C: Specificity for epitopes and absence of memory
options.D: Transferability and limited receptor diversity
options.E: Memory and transferability

questions.explanation: Innate: rapid, non-specific, pattern recognition, no memory, not transferable. Adaptive: acquired, specific, targeted, memory, transferable. A: These are innate properties. B: These are innate properties. C: Adaptive immunity has memory as its key feature. D: Adaptive receptor diversity is large.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a characteristic of adaptive immunity EXCEPT:

options.A: Specialization
options.B: Self-limitation
options.C: Clonal expansion
options.D: Pattern recognition
options.E: Self and non-self recognition

questions.explanation: Characteristics: specificity, diversity, memory, specialization, self and non-self recognition (self tolerance), self-limitation and clonal expansion. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: What underlies the specificity of adaptive immunity, the ability to distinguish even closely related molecules?

options.A: Each developing lymphocyte expresses several pattern recognition receptors, encoded in the germline
options.B: Each developing lymphocyte expresses one membrane receptor specificity, produced by antigen-receptor gene rearrangement
options.C: Each developing lymphocyte expresses one membrane receptor specificity, selected by the MHC haplotype of the pathogen
options.D: Each mature lymphocyte changes its receptor specificity after each new exposure to antigen
options.E: Each developing lymphocyte expresses two receptor specificities, one per parental chromosome

questions.explanation: Unlike innate cells with several PRRs, each developing lymphocyte expresses only one membrane receptor specificity and can distinguish slight differences between epitopes; this comes from antigen-receptor gene rearrangement. A: That describes innate cells. C: Specificity comes from receptor gene rearrangement. D: Rearrangement is irreversible; the clone keeps one specificity. E: The slide states one specificity per lymphocyte.

questions.stem: To what does the lecture attribute the diversity of adaptive immunity?

options.A: Variability in the structure of antigen-binding sites
options.B: Variability in the constant regions of the heavy chains
options.C: Polymorphism of MHC molecules between individuals
options.D: The large number of pattern recognition receptors per cell
options.E: Expansion of memory clones after each exposure

questions.explanation: Diversity (recognition of billions of different structures) is due to variability in the structures of the antigen-binding sites of lymphocyte receptors. B: Constant regions define class, not antigen recognition. C: MHC polymorphism is a separate property. D: That is innate recognition. E: That describes memory.

questions.stem: Compared with a primary response, how is a secondary immune response described, and what makes it possible?

options.A: Slower, larger and qualitatively identical; long-lived plasma cells from stimulated naive lymphocytes
options.B: More rapid, larger and often qualitatively different; long-lived memory cells from stimulated naive lymphocytes
options.C: More rapid, smaller and often qualitatively different; short-lived effector cells that persist between exposures
options.D: More rapid, larger and qualitatively identical; innate cells trained by the first exposure
options.E: Equally rapid, larger and often qualitatively different; a new rearrangement of receptor genes at each exposure

questions.explanation: Secondary responses are usually more rapid, larger and often qualitatively different. Stimulation of naive lymphocytes generates long-lived memory cells, and each exposure expands the antigen-specific clone. A: It is more rapid and often qualitatively different, and memory cells are the basis. C: It is larger, and memory cells are long-lived. D: Memory is a property of lymphocyte clones here. E: Rearrangement is not repeated; the clone expands.

questions.stem: The adaptive system responds in distinct ways to different classes of microbes, or to the same microbe at different stages of infection, maximizing the efficiency of defense. Which characteristic is this?

options.A: Specificity
options.B: Diversity
options.C: Self-limitation
options.D: Clonal expansion
options.E: Specialization

questions.explanation: Specialization: each type of immune response protects the host against a given class of microbe. A: Specificity is the distinction between closely related molecules. B: Diversity is the size of the recognition repertoire. C: That is waning of the response. D: That is proliferation of antigen-specific cells.

questions.stem: Which pair of definitions is correct?

options.A: Tolerance: unresponsiveness to self molecules; self-limitation: the response wanes with time, restoring homeostasis
options.B: Tolerance: the response wanes with time, restoring homeostasis; self-limitation: unresponsiveness to self molecules
options.C: Tolerance: unresponsiveness to foreign molecules; self-limitation: the response grows with each exposure
options.D: Tolerance: enhanced tissue resistance to damage; self-limitation: unresponsiveness to self molecules
options.E: Tolerance: unresponsiveness to self molecules; self-limitation: deletion of memory cells after infection

questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness to self molecules is tolerance. Self-limitation: the response wanes with time after antigenic stimulation, returning the system to its resting basal state (homeostasis). B: The two definitions are swapped. C: Tolerance concerns self, and growth with exposure is memory. D: The first is disease tolerance from the innate lecture. E: Memory cells are long-lived; self-limitation is return to the basal state.

questions.stem: Why do the progeny of an activated lymphocyte all carry the same antigen receptor?

options.A: Receptor gene rearrangement is repeated identically in each daughter cell
options.B: The antigen selects the same receptor in each daughter cell from several expressed
options.C: The MHC haplotype dictates the receptor sequence
options.D: Receptor gene rearrangement is an irreversible change in the lymphocyte's DNA
options.E: Costimulatory signals fix the receptor after activation

questions.explanation: The gene rearrangement that generates the receptor is irreversible and changes the lymphocyte's DNA, so all progeny express the same receptor: a clone. Because few lymphocytes recognize a given antigen, clonal expansion is needed. A: It is done once and inherited. B: Each lymphocyte expresses one specificity. C: MHC presents peptide; it does not encode the receptor. E: The receptor is fixed during development by rearrangement.

questions.stem: Which adaptive characteristic is exploited by vaccination, and failure of which one leads to autoimmunity?

options.A: Specialization is exploited by vaccination; failure of memory leads to autoimmunity
options.B: Memory is exploited by vaccination; failure of clonal expansion leads to autoimmunity
options.C: Memory is exploited by vaccination; failure of self tolerance leads to autoimmunity
options.D: Diversity is exploited by vaccination; failure of homeostasis leads to immunodeficiency
options.E: Self tolerance is exploited by vaccination; failure of memory leads to immune dysregulation

questions.explanation: The slide links memory with vaccination and self tolerance with immune dysregulation and autoimmunity. A: Vaccination relies on memory; autoimmunity on failed tolerance. B: Autoimmunity is linked to tolerance. D: Not the links shown. E: The links are reversed.

questions.stem: How do the antigen receptors of B cells and T cells differ?

options.A: Immunoglobulin exists as membrane-bound Ig (BCR) and is not secreted; the TCR is membrane-bound and also secreted
options.B: Immunoglobulin recognizes peptides on MHC; the TCR recognizes soluble or cell-bound native antigen
options.C: Immunoglobulin and TCR are both secreted after activation as effector molecules
options.D: Immunoglobulin exists as membrane-bound Ig (BCR) and secreted antibody; the TCR is never secreted
options.E: Immunoglobulin has one binding site; the TCR has two identical binding sites

questions.explanation: B-cell immunoglobulins recognize soluble or cell-bound antigen; soluble Ig = antibody, membrane-bound Ig = BCR. TCRs are made solely membrane-bound, associate with an intracellular signaling complex and recognize small peptides presented on MHC. A: The properties are swapped. B: The recognition modes are swapped. C: The TCR is never secreted. E: Antibody has two sites and the TCR one.

questions.stem: Which statement about antibody structure is correct?

options.A: 2 identical heavy and 2 different light chains; V regions bind antigen; the C region interacts with effector molecules and cells
options.B: 2 identical heavy and 2 identical light chains; V regions bind antigen; the C region interacts with effector molecules and cells
options.C: 2 identical heavy and 2 identical light chains; C regions bind antigen; the V region interacts with effector molecules and cells
options.D: 1 heavy and 1 light chain linked by a disulfide bond; one V domain and one C domain each; one binding site
options.E: 4 identical chains; V regions bind antigen at one site; the C region anchors the peptide groove

questions.explanation: Antibodies are Y-shaped, made of 4 chains (2 identical H, 2 identical L). The V regions at the ends of the arms bind antigen; the C region (stem) is far less variable and interacts with effector molecules and cells. A: The two light chains are identical. C: V and C roles are swapped. D: That resembles the TCR heterodimer. E: There are two chain types, two sites, and no peptide groove.

questions.stem: A patient's serum shows a kappa-to-lambda light chain ratio of 1:6. What is the normal human ratio, and what might the abnormal value indicate?

options.A: Normal is 2:1; an abnormal ratio might indicate a B-cell tumor
options.B: Normal is 1:2; an abnormal ratio might indicate a B-cell tumor
options.C: Normal is 2:1; an abnormal ratio might indicate a T-cell tumor
options.D: Normal is 1:1; an abnormal ratio might indicate complement deficiency
options.E: Normal is 3:1; an abnormal ratio might indicate failed class switching

questions.explanation: Light chains are either lambda or kappa; the κ/λ ratio is 2:1 in humans, and an abnormal ratio might indicate a B-cell tumor. B: The human κ/λ ratio is 2:1. C: Light chains are B-cell products. D: Neither part matches the slide. E: The ratio given is 2:1 and the association is B-cell tumor.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the five classes of immunoglobulin, and how are their heavy chains denoted?

options.A: The variable region of the heavy chain; five classes with heavy chains μ, α, δ, ε, γ
options.B: The constant region of the light chain; five classes with light chains κ and λ
options.C: The constant region of the heavy chain; five classes with heavy chains κ, λ, μ, α, γ
options.D: The number of antigen-binding sites; four classes with heavy chains μ, α, ε, γ
options.E: The constant region of the heavy chain; five classes with heavy chains μ, α, δ, ε, γ

questions.explanation: The 5 classes (IgM, IgA, IgG, IgE, IgD) differ in their constant region; heavy-chain isotypes are denoted μ, α, δ, ε, γ. A: Classes differ in the constant region. B: Light chain type does not define class. C: κ and λ are light chains. D: There are five classes including IgD (δ).

questions.stem: Having two identical antigen-binding sites increases the total strength of an antibody's interaction with antigen. Which terms apply?

options.A: Total strength from both sites is affinity; strength of a single site is avidity
options.B: Total strength from both sites is specificity; strength of a single site is affinity
options.C: Total strength from both sites is avidity; strength of a single site is affinity
options.D: Total strength from both sites is avidity; strength of a single site is valency
options.E: Total strength from both sites is diversity; strength of a single site is avidity

questions.explanation: Two sites increase the total strength of interaction (avidity); the strength of interaction of a single site is affinity. A: The terms are swapped. B: Specificity is not a strength measure. D: The single-site term is affinity. E: Diversity is repertoire size.

questions.stem: Which statement about somatic recombination of immunoglobulin genes matches the lecture?

options.A: Heavy chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 14; light chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 2 (κ) or 22
options.B: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 14; light chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 2 (κ) or 22
options.C: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 2; light chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 14 (κ) or 22
options.D: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 6; light chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 15
options.E: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 14; light chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 22 (κ) or 2

questions.explanation: V(D)J recombination: VDJ for IgH (locus on 14q) and VJ for IgL (κ on 2p, the other light chain on 22). Note: the slide writes "22 (Igγ)"; the light chain on chromosome 22 is lambda (λ). A: D segments belong to the heavy chain. C: The heavy-chain locus is on chromosome 14. D: Chromosomes 6 and 15 carry MHC and β2-microglobulin genes. E: Light chains have no D segment and κ is on chromosome 2.

questions.stem: What total number of B-cell receptors is predicted by the model cited in the lecture?

options.A: More than 10^8
options.B: About 30,000
options.C: More than 10^28
options.D: More than 10^18
options.E: About 10^6

questions.explanation: The total number of BCRs is predicted to exceed 10^18. A: The figure cited is 10^18. B: That is the number of identical TCRs on one T cell. C: The figure cited is 10^18. E: The figure cited is 10^18.

questions.stem: Which description of the T-cell receptor is correct?

options.A: A disulfide-linked heterodimer of TCRα and TCRβ with two binding sites; about 30,000 different copies per T cell
options.B: A non-covalent homodimer of two TCRβ chains with one binding site; about 3,000 identical copies per T cell
options.C: Four chains, two heavy and two light, with two binding sites; about 30,000 identical copies per T cell
options.D: A disulfide-linked heterodimer of TCRγ and TCRδ on most T cells; about 300,000 copies per T cell
options.E: A disulfide-linked heterodimer of TCRα and TCRβ with one binding site; about 30,000 identical copies per T cell

questions.explanation: Each T cell bears about 30,000 identical TCRs. Each receptor consists of TCRα and TCRβ (disulfide-linked heterodimer) with one binding site; each chain has one V and one C domain. A minority of T cells bear an alternative receptor. A: There is one binding site and the copies are identical. B: It is an αβ heterodimer and the number is about 30,000. C: That is antibody structure. D: A minority of T cells bear the alternative receptor.

questions.stem: During T-cell development, which marker is expressed by all T cells as part of the TCR complex, and what happens if gene rearrangement of the β or α chain fails?

options.A: CD3; the cell dies
options.B: CD4; the cell becomes an NK cell
options.C: CD8; the cell dies
options.D: CD3; the cell expresses both CD4 and CD8 permanently
options.E: CD59; the cell becomes a γδ T cell

questions.explanation: Gene rearrangement occurs for the β chain and the α chain; failure leads to cell death. All T cells express CD3 (part of the T-cell receptor complex); once fully mature they express CD4 or CD8. B: CD4 marks helper cells after maturation; failure leads to death. C: CD8 marks mature cytotoxic T cells. D: Failure of rearrangement leads to death. E: CD59 is a complement regulator.

questions.stem: Which statement about NKT cells matches the lecture?

options.A: They eliminate tumor cells and stressed cells, help avoid autoimmunity, and recognize peptide on MHC II
options.B: They carry a unique TCR, are found at mucosal and epithelial sites, and promote wound healing
options.C: They eliminate tumor and stressed cells, help avoid autoimmunity, and do not recognize MHC II
options.D: They suppress other T cells and are the main mediators of self tolerance
options.E: They kill infected cells after priming and express CD8

questions.explanation: NKT cells: role in eliminating tumor cells and cells stressed by trauma or temperature, role in avoiding autoimmunity; they do not recognize MHC II. A: The slide stresses they do not recognize MHC II. B: That describes γδ T cells. D: That suggests regulatory T cells. E: That describes cytotoxic T cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about γδ T cells is correct?

options.A: Low-abundance cells at mucosal and epithelial sites with a unique TCR; an innate component
options.B: Abundant cells in lymph nodes with a unique TCR; a component of adaptive immunity that provides memory
options.C: Low-abundance cells at mucosal sites without a TCR; a component of innate immunity that kills by perforin
options.D: Low-abundance cells in the thymus with the αβ TCR; they suppress inflammation to promote tolerance
options.E: Circulating helper cells with a unique TCR that recognize peptide on MHC II and activate B cells

questions.explanation: γδ T cells express a unique TCR, are of low abundance (mucosal and epithelial sites), are a component of innate immunity, induce inflammation to promote infection clearance and promote wound healing. B: They are of low abundance, at mucosal/epithelial sites, and counted as innate. C: They do express a (unique) TCR. D: They induce inflammation to promote infection clearance. E: That is the helper T-cell role.

questions.stem: Which statement about antigens is correct?

options.A: They are typically lipids or nucleic acids; proteins can combine with these to form complex antigens such as LPS
options.B: They are typically proteins; polysaccharides cannot produce an immune response
options.C: Typically proteins, peptides or polysaccharides; lipids and nucleic acids can join them, as in LPS
options.D: They are small molecules that need a carrier protein to produce a response
options.E: They are surface features of a molecule that are bound by antibody

questions.explanation: An antigen is a substance capable of producing an immune response, recognized as non-self; typically proteins, peptides or polysaccharides. Lipids and nucleic acids can combine with them to form more complex antigens like lipopolysaccharide. A: Typical antigens are proteins, peptides or polysaccharides. B: Polysaccharides are listed as typical antigens. D: That defines haptens. E: That defines an epitope.

questions.stem: A small drug molecule provokes an immune response only after binding a serum protein. Which terms describe the drug, the complex, and the surface feature of the complex bound by antibody?

options.A: Epitope; adduct; hapten
options.B: Hapten; epitope; adduct
options.C: Adduct; hapten; epitope
options.D: Hapten; adduct; epitope
options.E: Autoantigen; adduct; native antigen

questions.explanation: Haptens are small molecules that trigger a response only when combined with a carrier protein; the hapten-carrier complex is an adduct. An epitope is a molecular surface feature of an antigen that can be bound by an antibody. A: The small molecule is the hapten; the bound feature is the epitope. B: The hapten-carrier complex is the adduct. C: The complex, not the drug, is the adduct. E: The drug is not a self protein.

questions.stem: Match the antigen types with their definitions.

options.A: Endogenous antigen: normal self protein attacked when tolerance is altered; autoantigen: generated within cells by intracellular infection
options.B: Endogenous antigen: generated within cells by metabolism or intracellular infection; autoantigen: normal self protein attacked when tolerance is altered
options.C: Exogenous antigen: generated within cells by viral infection; endogenous antigen: enters by inhalation, ingestion or injection
options.D: Neoantigen: normal self protein in a tumor; autoantigen: tumor-specific mutated protein
options.E: Native antigen: peptide already processed by an APC; endogenous antigen: unprocessed protein in plasma

questions.explanation: Exogenous antigens enter from outside; endogenous antigens are generated within previously normal cells (metabolism, viral or intracellular bacterial infection); autoantigens are normal self proteins attacked when tolerance is altered. A: The definitions are swapped. C: The definitions are swapped. D: Neoantigens come from tumor-specific mutations. E: A native antigen is not yet processed.

questions.stem: Which statement about tumor antigens (neoantigens) is correct?

options.A: They result from a tumor-specific mutation and are hidden from MHC molecules, so tumors cannot be recognized
options.B: They are normal self proteins presented on MHC class I, and tumors are reliably killed once they appear
options.C: They result from viral infection of normal cells and are presented on MHC class II exclusively
options.D: They are unprocessed proteins that activate T cells directly without MHC
options.E: They result from a tumor-specific mutation and are expressed on MHC class I and II, yet many tumors evade recognition

questions.explanation: Neoantigens result from a tumor-specific mutation during malignant transformation; despite expressing them on MHC class I and II, many tumors have developed ways to evade recognition and killing. A: They are expressed on MHC I and II. B: They are mutated, and many tumors evade killing. C: They arise from mutation in malignant transformation. D: T cells need processed peptide on MHC.

questions.stem: How do B cells and T cells differ in handling a native antigen?

options.A: B cells can be activated by a native antigen without processing; T cells need it digested and processed by APCs
options.B: T cells can be activated by a native antigen without processing; B cells need it digested and processed by APCs
options.C: Both need the antigen digested by APCs and presented on MHC
options.D: Both bind native antigen directly through membrane immunoglobulin
options.E: B cells bind native antigen on MHC II; T cells bind native antigen on MHC I

questions.explanation: A native antigen is not yet processed by an APC. T cells cannot bind native antigens; B cells can be activated by native ones without prior processing. B: The cell types are swapped. C: B cells bind native antigen. D: T cells use the TCR and need processed peptide on MHC. E: Native antigen is unprocessed and not MHC-bound.

questions.stem: Protein antigens of microbes entering through skin, gut or airways are captured mainly by which cells, and where are immune responses initiated?

options.A: Dendritic cells; antigens are concentrated in the primary lymphoid organs
options.B: Neutrophils; antigens are concentrated in the bone marrow
options.C: Dendritic cells; antigens are concentrated in secondary lymphoid organs
options.D: B cells; antigens are concentrated at the site of entry
options.E: Macrophages; antigens are concentrated in the thymus

questions.explanation: Protein antigens are captured mainly by dendritic cells and concentrated in the peripheral (secondary) lymphoid organs, where immune responses are initiated. A: Responses start in secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organs. B: Dendritic cells are the main capturing cells. D: Capture is mainly by dendritic cells with transport to lymphoid organs. E: The thymus is a primary organ.

questions.stem: Why is cell-mediated immunity needed against viruses and other intracellular microbes?

options.A: Antibodies cannot neutralize extracellular microbes and toxins, so T cells must do it
options.B: B cells do not recognize protein antigens, so T cells must respond
options.C: Intracellular microbes lack epitopes, so pattern recognition must take over
options.D: Complement destroys antibodies inside infected cells
options.E: Inside host cells they are inaccessible to antibodies, so infected cells are killed

questions.explanation: Humoral immunity (B cells, antibodies) neutralizes extracellular microbes and toxins. Intracellular microbes and viruses are inside host cells and phagocytes, inaccessible to antibodies, so T cells kill infected cells or activate phagocytes. A: Extracellular microbes and toxins are the target of humoral immunity. B: B cells recognize native protein antigens. C: Not stated; the issue is access. D: Not the reason given.

questions.stem: Which cells are the classical APCs, and what do they do?

options.A: Dendritic cells, T cells and macrophages; they process protein antigen into peptides presented on MHC II to B cells
options.B: Dendritic cells, B cells and macrophages; they process protein antigen into peptides presented on MHC II to T cells
options.C: Dendritic cells, B cells and neutrophils; they present native antigen on MHC I to T cells
options.D: Macrophages, NK cells and B cells; they process protein antigen into peptides presented on MHC II
options.E: Dendritic cells, B cells and macrophages; they secrete antibody against the processed peptide

questions.explanation: Classical APCs are dendritic cells, B cells and macrophages: a heterogeneous group that processes a protein antigen into peptides and presents them on MHC II for recognition by T cells. A: B cells, not T cells, are classical APCs, and presentation is to T cells. C: Neutrophils are not listed, and antigen is processed onto MHC II. D: NK cells are not APCs. E: Antibody secretion is not their defining role here.

questions.stem: After collecting antigen in a peripheral tissue, where does an APC go?

options.A: To the bone marrow, a primary lymphoid organ where naive T cells are generated
options.B: To the thymus, where naive T cells mature
options.C: It stays in the tissue and waits for memory T cells
options.D: To the draining lymph node, where naive T cells circulate
options.E: To the bloodstream, where it presents antigen to neutrophils

questions.explanation: APCs are bone marrow-derived, seed peripheral tissues, collect antigens and traffic to secondary lymphoid organs (they drain to the neighboring lymph node where naive T cells circulate). A: APCs traffic to secondary lymphoid organs. B: The thymus is a primary organ. C: APCs drain to lymph nodes. E: Presentation is to lymphocytes in lymphoid organs.

questions.stem: Which cells express MHC class I and which express MHC class II?

options.A: Class I: nucleated cells and mature erythrocytes, but not platelets; class II: monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells
options.B: Class I: nucleated cells and platelets, but not mature erythrocytes; class II: monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells
options.C: Class I: antigen-presenting cells; class II: nucleated cells and platelets
options.D: Class I: nucleated cells and platelets; class II: T cells, NK cells and neutrophils
options.E: Class I: lymphocytes; class II: monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and mature erythrocytes

questions.explanation: MHC class I is on nucleated cells and platelets but not mature erythrocytes; MHC class II is on antigen-presenting cells: monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells. A: Platelets express class I; mature erythrocytes do not. C: The classes are swapped. D: Class II is on APCs. E: Mature erythrocytes lack MHC.

questions.stem: On which chromosome is the HLA system, and which coreceptor binds each MHC class?

options.A: Chromosome 6; CD4 on helper T cells binds MHC I and CD8 on cytotoxic T cells binds MHC II
options.B: Chromosome 15; CD4 on helper T cells binds MHC II and CD8 on cytotoxic T cells binds MHC I
options.C: Chromosome 14; CD8 on helper T cells binds MHC II and CD4 on cytotoxic T cells binds MHC I
options.D: Chromosome 6; CD4 on helper T cells binds MHC II and CD8 on cytotoxic T cells binds MHC I
options.E: Chromosome 2; CD3 on T cells binds both MHC classes

questions.explanation: HLA genes are on chromosome 6. MHC II is bound by CD4 on helper T cells; MHC I by CD8 on cytotoxic T cells. A: The coreceptors are swapped. B: Chromosome 15 carries the β2-microglobulin gene. C: Chromosome 14 carries the heavy-chain locus, and the cells are mislabeled. E: CD3 is part of the TCR complex.

questions.stem: Which listing of HLA loci is correct?

options.A: Class I major: DR, DP, DQ; minor: HLA-DM and HLA-DO. Class II major: A, B, C; minor: E, F, G
options.B: Class I major: A, B, C; minor: HLA-DM and HLA-DO. Class II major: DR, DP, DQ; minor: E, F, G
options.C: Class I major: A, B, DR; minor: E, F. Class II major: C, DP, DQ; minor: DM, DO, G
options.D: Class I major: A, B, C; minor: E, F, G. Class II major: DR, DP, DQ; minor: TNF and heat shock protein genes
options.E: Class I major: A, B, C; minor: HLA-E, HLA-F, HLA-G. Class II major: DR, DP, DQ; minor: HLA-DM and HLA-DO

questions.explanation: Class I: major loci HLA-A, -B, -C and minor HLA-E, -F, -G. Class II: major HLA-DR, -DP, -DQ and minor HLA-DM, -DO. A: The classes are swapped. B: The minor loci are swapped. C: Loci are mixed between classes. D: Those genes lie in the class III region.

questions.stem: What does the HLA class III region contain?

options.A: The minor class II loci HLA-DM and HLA-DO
options.B: The β2-microglobulin gene
options.C: Immune and non-immune genes, such as TNF
options.D: The immunoglobulin heavy-chain V, D and J segments
options.E: The minor class I loci HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G

questions.explanation: The class III region includes both immune and non-immune associated genes like the tumour necrosis factor gene and heat shock proteins' genes. A: These are class II. B: That gene is on chromosome 15. D: Those are on chromosome 14. E: These are class I.

questions.stem: How do MHC class I and class II differ in structure?

options.A: Class I: one α chain with a smaller non-MHC chain encoded on chromosome 15; class II: α and β chains, both spanning the membrane
options.B: Class I: α and β chains, both spanning the membrane; class II: one α chain with a smaller non-MHC chain encoded on chromosome 15
options.C: Class I: one α chain covalently bound to a chain encoded on chromosome 6; class II: two α chains
options.D: Class I: a single α chain with no partner; class II: α and β chains covalently linked, one spanning the membrane
options.E: Class I: two MHC-encoded chains; class II: one MHC-encoded chain plus a chain encoded on chromosome 15

questions.explanation: MHC I: one α chain (chromosome 6) non-covalently associated with a smaller, non-MHC-encoded chain from chromosome 15 (β2-microglobulin; the slide writes "β-macroglobulin"). MHC II: non-covalent complex of MHC-encoded α and β chains, both spanning the membrane. B: The classes are swapped. C: The association is non-covalent, the small chain is on chromosome 15, and class II is αβ. D: Class I has a second small chain, and class II chains are non-covalently associated and both span the membrane. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: In both MHC classes, which domains form the peptide-binding groove?

options.A: The membrane-proximal domains; the membrane-distal domains resemble Ig domains
options.B: The transmembrane domains; the cytoplasmic tails resemble Ig domains
options.C: The membrane-distal domains; the membrane-proximal domains resemble Ig domains
options.D: The β2-microglobulin chain in class I and the β chain by itself in class II
options.E: The membrane-distal domains of class I and the membrane-proximal domains of class II

questions.explanation: The membrane-proximal domains resemble Ig domains, while the membrane-distal domains fold together to create a groove. A: Reversed. B: The groove is extracellular and distal. D: The groove is formed by distal domains folding together. E: It is membrane-distal in both.

questions.stem: MHC class II molecules present antigens from which source, and how long is the bound peptide on the slide?

options.A: From inside the cell; a 14–20 amino acid long peptide
options.B: From outside the cell; a 4–6 amino acid long peptide
options.C: From the cytosol via TAP; a 30–40 amino acid long peptide
options.D: From outside the cell; an intact native protein
options.E: From outside the cell; a 14–20 amino acid long peptide

questions.explanation: Cells engulf and destroy pathogens and present antigens to CD4+ helper T cells on MHC class II, which holds a 14–20 amino acid long peptide. A: Class II presents antigens from outside the cell. B: The slide gives 14–20. C: TAP serves class I. D: MHC binds peptides.

questions.stem: An individual expresses, on every expressing cell, the HLA products inherited from both parents. Which term names this, and which term names the existence of multiple alleles of each gene?

options.A: Codominant expression; polymorphic
options.B: Polygenic expression; polymorphic
options.C: Codominant expression; polygenic
options.D: Polymorphic expression; codominant
options.E: Dominant expression; heterozygous

questions.explanation: MHC is polygenic (several genes), polymorphic (multiple alleles of each gene; most individuals are heterozygous at each locus) and codominant (alleles expressed from both haplotypes, products of all alleles on all expressing cells). B: Polygenic means several genes. C: Multiple alleles of each gene is polymorphism. D: The terms are swapped. E: Both haplotypes are expressed, and the term for many alleles is polymorphic.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a feature of peptide–MHC interaction EXCEPT:

options.A: Each MHC molecule displays one peptide at a time
options.B: Each MHC molecule binds one specific peptide with a fast off-rate
options.C: Many different peptides can bind the same MHC molecule
options.D: Peptides are acquired during intracellular assembly
options.E: Stable surface expression of an MHC molecule requires bound peptide

questions.explanation: Features: broad specificity, one peptide at a time, MHC binds only peptides, peptide is loaded during intracellular assembly, stable surface expression requires peptide, and a very slow off-rate. A: A listed feature. C: A listed feature (broad specificity). D: A listed feature. E: A listed feature.

questions.stem: A virus replicates in the cytosol of an epithelial cell. Put the endogenous presentation steps in order: (1) transport of peptides into the ER by TAP, (2) proteasomal degradation of ubiquitinated protein, (3) surface expression to CD8+ T cells, (4) assembly of peptide–class I complexes.
questions.explanation: Endogenous pathway: cytosolic proteins are ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome, peptides are transported into the ER by TAP, loaded onto class I, and expressed on the surface for CD8+ T cells. MHC class I molecules do not leave the ER unless they bind peptides. A: Proteasomal degradation precedes TAP transport. B: Peptides must enter the ER before loading. C: Loading in the ER precedes surface expression. E: Assembly follows peptide generation and transport.

questions.stem: In the exogenous pathway, what occupies the class II molecule before peptide loading, and which molecule is shown at the exchange step?

options.A: CLIP; HLA-DM
options.B: CLIP; TAP
options.C: β2-microglobulin; HLA-DM
options.D: Tapasin; the proteasome
options.E: Ubiquitin; HLA-DO

questions.explanation: Exogenous pathway: extracellular protein is taken into vesicles and processed in endosomes/lysosomes; class II made in the ER travels to endosomes, where CLIP is exchanged for peptide with HLA-DM, and the complex is shown to CD4+ helper T cells. B: TAP transports cytosolic peptides for class I. C: β2-microglobulin is part of class I. D: These belong to the class I pathway. E: Ubiquitin tags cytosolic proteins for the proteasome.

questions.stem: In the innate versus adaptive comparison table, which row is correct?

options.A: Receptors: adaptive are germline encoded; innate are generated by somatic gene rearrangement, with a rapid response
options.B: Distribution: innate is clonal; adaptive is non-clonal, with cells of a class identical
options.C: Potency: innate is high; adaptive is limited and lower
options.D: Memory: innate has memory as its key feature; adaptive lacks it
options.E: Receptors: innate are germline encoded; adaptive are generated by somatic gene rearrangement, with a slow response (1–2 weeks)

questions.explanation: Innate: rapid, limited potency, low specificity, limited germline-encoded receptors, non-clonal, no memory. Adaptive: slow (1–2 weeks), high potency, specific, receptors from somatic gene rearrangement, clonal, memory. A: Reversed. B: Reversed. C: Reversed. D: Reversed.

questions.stem: Which set contains effector molecules assigned to innate immunity in the comparison table?

options.A: Complement, antibodies, chemokines and antimicrobial peptides
options.B: Granzyme, perforin, antibodies and cytokines
options.C: Acute-phase reactants, antibodies and growth factors
options.D: Complement, acute-phase reactants and antimicrobial peptides
options.E: Complement, T-cell receptors and antimicrobial peptides

questions.explanation: Innate effector molecules: complement, acute-phase reactants, chemokines, cytokines, growth factors, antimicrobial peptides. Adaptive: antibodies, cytotoxic molecules (granzyme, perforin), cytokines. A: Antibodies are adaptive effector molecules. B: These are listed under adaptive immunity. C: Antibodies are adaptive. E: TCRs are receptors, not listed effector molecules.

questions.stem: According to the comparison table, what are the effects on the host of innate versus adaptive responses?

options.A: Innate: no effect on homeostasis and minimal injury; adaptive: altered homeostasis and bystander activation
options.B: Innate: reactivity against self; adaptive: bystander activation
options.C: Innate: altered homeostasis and bystander activation; adaptive: no effect on homeostasis and minimal injury
options.D: Innate: minimal injury; adaptive: reactivity against self
options.E: Innate: altered homeostasis; adaptive: altered homeostasis with memory loss

questions.explanation: Table: innate responses cause altered homeostasis and bystander activation; adaptive responses have no effect on homeostasis and cause minimal injury; neither is reactive against self. A: Reversed. B: The table lists no self-reactivity for either. D: Neither matches the table. E: Adaptive has no effect on homeostasis in the table.

questions.stem: T-cell activation requires two signals. Which pair is correct?

options.A: Signal 1: costimulatory molecules binding their ligands; signal 2: TCR ligation with its antigen on MHC
options.B: Signal 1: TCR ligation with antigen on MHC; signal 2: costimulatory molecules binding ligands on the APC
options.C: Signal 1: TCR ligation with native antigen; signal 2: antibody binding to the T cell
options.D: Signal 1: BCR ligation with antigen; signal 2: complement receptor binding
options.E: Signal 1: CD4 or CD8 binding MHC; signal 2: cytokine secretion by the T cell

questions.explanation: Signal 1: ligation of the TCR with its antigen presented on MHC molecules. Signal 2: ligation of costimulatory molecules on T cells with their respective ligands on the APC. A: The order is reversed. C: The TCR sees peptide on MHC, and antibody is not signal 2. D: That is not T-cell activation. E: The signals are TCR–peptide-MHC and costimulation.
